extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent prosecutors/attorneys as secondary audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and supporting rejections under 35 U.S.C. §101 (subject matter eligibility), including how to identify judicial exceptions, evaluate additional claim elements (Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B), evidentiary support requirements, and required form paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and explain the judicial exception recited in the claim (Step 2A Prong One)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subject matter eligibility rejection should point to the specific claim limitation(s) that recites (i.e., sets forth or describes) the judicial exception. The rejection must explain why those claim limitations set forth or describe a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making a rejection, identify the judicial exception by referring to what is recited (i.e., set forth or described) in the claim and explain why it is considered an exception. If the claim describes but does not expressly set forth the judicial exception, the rejection must also explain what subject matter those limitations describe and why the described subject matter is a judicial exception. See MPEP § 2106.04 for more information about Step 2A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify abstract idea as recited and justify grouping or use tentative procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: When the examiner has determined the claim recites an abstract idea, the rejection should identify the abstract idea as it is recited (i.e., set forth or described) in the claim, and explain why it falls within one of the groupings of abstract ideas (mathematical concepts, mental processes, or certain methods of organizing human activity) enumerated in MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternatively, provide justification for why a specific limitation(s) recited in the claim is being treated as an abstract idea if it does not fall within the groupings (use the 'tentative abstract idea' procedure). While not required, the explanation may include citing an appropriate court decision that supports the identification. Examiners should be familiar with any cited decision and avoid relying on language taken out of context or on non-precedential decisions unless facts uniquely match. A sample explanation: 'The claim recites the step of comparing collected information to a predefined threshold, which is an act of evaluating information that can be practically performed in the human mind. Thus, this step is an abstract idea in the "mental process" grouping.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify law of nature or natural phenomenon as recited and provide reasoned rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: When the examiner has determined the claim recites a law of nature or a natural phenomenon, the rejection should identify the law of nature or natural phenomenon as it is recited (i.e., set forth or described) in the claim and explain using a reasoned rationale why it is considered a law of nature or natural phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2106.04(b) for more information. Sample explanations: 'The claim recites the correlation of X, and X is a law of nature because it describes a consequence of natural processes in the human body...' or 'The claim recites X, which is a natural phenomenon because it occurs in nature and exists in principle apart from any human action.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify product of nature exception and explain lack of markedly different characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: When the examiner has determined the claim recites a product of nature, the rejection should identify the exception as it is recited in the claim, and explain using a reasoned rationale why the product does not have markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2106.04(b) and § 2106.04(c) (markedly different characteristics analysis). Sample explanation: 'The claim recites X, which as explained in the specification was isolated from naturally occurring Y. X is a nature-based product, so it is compared to its closest naturally occurring counterpart (X in its natural state) to determine if it has markedly different characteristics. Because there is no indication in the record that isolation of X has resulted in a marked difference in structure, function, or other properties as compared to its counterpart, X is a product of nature exception.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify additional claim elements and evaluate integration/amounting to significantly more (Step 2A Prong Two & Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: After identifying the judicial exception, identify any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception and explain why they do not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application and do not add significantly more to the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The explanation should address additional elements both individually and in combination when determining whether the claim as a whole recites eligible subject matter. It is important to remember that a new combination of steps may be patent eligible even though all steps were individually known (Diamond v. Diehr). Thus, address combinations carefully because combined additional elements may meaningfully limit the judicial exception. A rejection should be made only if it is readily apparent to an examiner relying on expertise in the art in the Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B inquiries. When making a rejection, explain the rationale so applicant can effectively respond. See MPEP §§ 2106.04(d) and 2106.05 for considerations that qualify or do not qualify as integrating an exception or providing significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support findings that elements are well-understood, routine, conventional (evidentiary requirement for Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner concludes particular claim limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional activities (Step 2B), the rejection should support this conclusion in writing with a factual determination using one or more specified options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should not assert that an additional element is well-understood, routine, or conventional unless they find and expressly support the rejection in writing with one or more of the following: (A) citation to an express statement in the specification or applicant's prosecution statements demonstrating the element is well-understood/routine/conventional; (B) citation to one or more court decisions noting the well-understood/routine/conventional nature (ensuring the claim limitations match the court's); (C) citation to a publication that demonstrates the element is widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant field; or (D) a statement that the examiner is taking official notice of the well-understood/routine/conventional nature (used only when certain based on personal knowledge). See Subsection III and MPEP § 2106.05(d) for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: No evidence required to identify a judicial exception (Step 2A Prong One)
rubrics_metrics.description: When performing the analysis at Step 2A Prong One, it is sufficient for the examiner to provide a reasoned rationale that identifies the judicial exception recited in the claim and explains why it is considered a judicial exception; there is no requirement to rely on evidence such as publications or affidavits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Federal Circuit decisions that characterize eligibility as a question of law (e.g., Rapid Litig. Mgmt., OIP Techs., DDR Holdings). Examples show courts identifying abstract ideas without relying on evidence. Thus, for Step 2A Prong One, a reasoned rationale is sufficient and evidence is not required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary threshold for Step 2A Prong Two / Step 2B only when asserting well-understood/routine/conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: At Step 2A Prong Two or Step 2B, there is no requirement for evidence to support findings that the exception is not integrated into a practical application or that additional elements do not amount to significantly more, unless the examiner asserts that additional limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting well-understood/routine/conventional, the examiner must support that assertion using one of the options (A-D) described in the evidentiary requirements (citation to spec/prosecution, court decisions, publications, or official notice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why generic computer components or generic computing functions do not meaningfully limit the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: For claim limitations that recite a generic computer component performing generic computer functions at a high level of generality, examiners can explain why these generic computing functions do not meaningfully limit the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep in mind courts have found computer-implemented processes to be significantly more than an abstract idea where generic components in combination perform non-generic functions (DDR Holdings). See MPEP § 2106.05(f) for generic computing functions that the courts have found to be mere instructions to implement a judicial exception on a computer, and MPEP § 2106.05(d) for information on well-understood/routine/conventional activities. Examples: merely using the Internet to gather data or storing data in a final step may be insignificant extra-solution activity that does not add a meaningful limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address insignificant extra-solution activity and mere field/technological environment limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: For claim limitations that add insignificant extra-solution activity to the judicial exception (e.g., mere data gathering) or that generally link the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use, examiners should explain why they do not meaningfully limit the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: adding a final step of storing data to a process that only recites computing a mathematical relationship does not add a meaningful limitation; employing well-known computer functions to execute an abstract idea, even when limiting to one environment, may be insufficient (Parker v. Flook). See MPEP § 2106.05(g) and § 2106.05(h) for more information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best practice: consult specification to suggest claim amendments to overcome §101 rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: In the event a rejection is made, it is a best practice for the examiner to consult the specification to determine if there are elements that could be added to the claim to make it eligible and identify those elements in the Office action as a way to overcome the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If such elements exist in the specification, the examiner should identify and suggest them in the Office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact prosecution: perform complete examination under other patentability requirements and state non-cumulative reasons in first Office action
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the principles of compact prosecution, regardless of whether a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 is made, a complete examination should be made for every claim under each of the other patentability requirements (35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112, and utility, inventorship, double patenting, and non-statutory double patenting). Examiners should state all non-cumulative reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement ensures a complete record and supports efficient prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of specified form paragraphs for §101 rejections and procedural ordering
rubrics_metrics.description: Use designated form paragraphs (e.g., 7.04.01, 7.05, 7.05.01, 7.05.016, 7.05.017) for rejections based on subject matter eligibility and nonstatutory rejections, and follow required ordering (e.g., 7.04.01 must precede first use of 35 U.S.C. 101 in first actions and final rejections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ¶ 7.04.01: Statement of statutory basis (35 U.S.C. 101) — must precede first use of 101. ¶ 7.05: Rejection heading only — must be preceded by 7.04.01 and followed by detailed explanation using other form paragraphs. ¶ 7.05.01: Rejection nonstatutory (not one of four statutory categories) — explain why not within process/machine/manufacture/composition. ¶ 7.05.016: Rejection directed to a judicial exception without significantly more — identify type of exception, how recited in claim, why not integrated, why additional elements do not amount to significantly more. For tentative abstract ideas, include ¶ 7.05.017 and TC Director signature. Follow examiner notes and bracket guidance when filling these paragraphs.
